warli.history: One of the oldest tribal art forms in India, practiced by the Warli tribe for centuries, traditionally painted on mud walls using rice paste.
warli.symbolism: Depicts daily life, nature, and rituals using basic geometric shapes — circles, triangles, and lines representing the sun, mountains, and human figures.

madhubani.history: Also known as Mithila painting, traditionally created by women on freshly plastered mud walls and floors, dating back centuries.
madhubani.symbolism: Features intricate patterns, natural motifs, and mythological themes, often depicting Hindu deities and nature.

pichwai.history: Traditionally painted on cloth and hung behind the idol of Lord Krishna (Shrinathji) in temples.
pichwai.symbolism: Rich, detailed depictions of Krishna's life, often featuring cows, lotus flowers, and elaborate festival scenes.

kalighat.history: Emerged in the 19th century near the Kalighat temple, evolving from religious scroll painting into bold, satirical social commentary.
kalighat.symbolism: Characterized by bold, sweeping brushstrokes and flat colors, depicting deities as well as social and political themes.

kangra.history: Flourished in the 18th century under the patronage of the Kangra royal court, part of the broader Pahari painting tradition.
kangra.symbolism: Delicate, lyrical style often depicting romantic and devotional themes, especially stories of Radha and Krishna.

kerala_mural.history: An ancient temple art form found on the walls of temples and palaces across Kerala, dating back over a thousand years.
kerala_mural.symbolism: Vivid, elaborate depictions of Hindu mythology using a distinct palette of earthy reds, yellows, greens, and blacks.

mandana_art.history: Traditionally drawn on floors and walls of homes during festivals and special occasions using red ochre and white chalk.
mandana_art.symbolism: Geometric and floral patterns believed to bring good fortune, often drawn fresh for weddings and religious ceremonies.

gond.history: Practiced by the Gond tribe, one of India's largest tribal communities, traditionally painted on walls and floors.
gond.symbolism: Dense, dotted patterns depicting nature, animals, and folklore, believed to bring good luck when displayed in homes.
